Security personnel stand at the scene of a destroyed building following a drone attack on a neighbourhood in the Sudanese capital Khartoum on November 22, 2026 [AFP]By Al Jazeera Staff and AFPPublished On 22 Nov 202622 Nov 2026
Drone attacks blamed on Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have killed four people in and around the capital, Khartoum, and damaged a United Nations building, according to local reports and UN officials.
The attacks early on Sunday struck residential areas as Sudanese air defences responded to drones reportedly targeting government buildings and Khartoum’s airport.

The strikes have raised fresh concerns about the growing danger to civilians and aid workers as Sudan‘s war increasingly relies on drones.
Explosions were heard across the capital between approximately 2am (00:00 GMT) and 4:30am (02:30 GMT), according to witnesses cited by the AFP news agency, as the army attempted to intercept the drones.
Al Jazeera’s AlMigdad Alruhaid reported from the city of Omdurman, across the Nile from Khartoum, that three people were killed and nine wounded when a drone struck a home in northern Omdurman.
A child was also killed in a separate attack south of the capital.
In the village of Jebel Aulia, about 45km (28 miles) south of Khartoum, a witness told AFP that a drone hit the home of a mosque official who calls worshippers to prayer. item.title: The Drugs Don’t Work
item.description:
play video
play video
Video Duration 47 minutes 26 seconds play-arrow
47:26
A look at how antibiotic overuse could fuel superbugs, killing eight million people annually by 2050.Read more
The challenges posed by antimicrobial resistance show where its impact is most acutely and tragically manifested: infant mortality in the developing world, specifically in sub-Saharan Africa. This film shows what these bland statistics mean in real terms to the health workers and families affected, following them as they struggle to fight this battle with low-tech solutions.
The Drugs Don’t Work follows the battle to the United Kingdom and examines how and why penicillin, the world’s most successful antibiotic, was invented. It then examines why pharmaceutical companies like GlaxoSmithKline are struggling to produce novel solutions to the problem of antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
The film also explores the cutting edge of academic research at British universities and hospitals supported by the power of the UK-based tech company DeepMind, and features academics and advocates who are devoting their lives to solving the problem. Returning to Africa, it shows how local innovation and the tools offered by the developed world are now saving lives and contributing to the global battle against AMR – an effort that could ultimately save millions of lives.Published On 22 Nov 202622 Nov 2026

At least four people have been killed and police stations, banks and even the ancestral home of the former interim leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner, Muhammad Yunus, have been attacked in a week of violence.

After weeks of careful and detailed planning, Mexican special forces have captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as El Chapo Isidro, a notorious alleged cartel leader on the FBI’s 10 most-wanted list.
Authorities said on Saturday Meza Flores was arrested at a compound in Guasave, in the northwestern state of Sinaloa, following a stealth operation that left four members of the security forces and seven suspected gunmen dead.

Who is Meza Flores?
Meza Flores, 44, is believed to be the leader of the Los Mazatlecos gang, based in Guasave, an agricultural area in Sinaloa.
The group was formerly part of the now-extinct Beltran Leyva Cartel but has operated independently since 2013. Meza Flores had long been subject to arrest in Mexico on charges of organised crime.

The new launcher is capable of carrying and firing two liquid-fuel missiles simultaneously, according to Iranian state media [Screengrab/Reuters]By Urooba JamalPublished On 22 Nov 202622 Nov 2026
Iran is putting its upgraded missile systems and underground military facilities on display, delivering a defiant message that it still has significant military capabilities despite US-Israeli attacks.
The latest showcase included a dual-missile launcher capable of firing two liquid-fuelled missiles simultaneously, according to state media broadcasting footage of military commanders touring an underground missile facility.
Officials insisted Iran has strengthened its missile and air-defence capabilities since previous rounds of fighting, including the launch of the US-Israel war in late February. Still, Iran is under mounting economic pressure from a naval blockade imposed by the United States that has disrupted its oil exports.
Here’s everything to know about the new dual-missile launcher and Iran’s “missile city”:
What is the new launcher?
Iran has developed a range of ballistic and cruise missiles over the past three decades.
The new dual-missile launcher was unveiled as Major-General Ahmad Vahidi, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), toured the underground facility on Saturday.
The IRGC aerospace force flaunted its range of upgraded missiles and military equipment, including the launcher, which is designed to carry and fire two liquid-fuelled missiles simultaneously, according to state broadcaster IRIB.
Liquid-fuelled missiles are launched vertically and offer speed-control capabilities, which can aid in overcoming air defence systems, IRIB reported.

Members of the Iraqi armed group Kataib Hezbollah patrol the roadside in Jurf al-Sakhar, Babil province, Iraq, November 20, 2026 [Alaa Al-Marjani/Reuters]By Rached El-Moctar and Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 22 Nov 202622 Nov 2026
The entry of Iraqi government forces into Jurf al-Sakhar, a town 60km (37 miles) southwest of Baghdad long held by the Iran-backed armed group Kataib Hezbollah, has raised questions about the future of Iraqi militias in the country.
A deal reached between Iraqi authorities and Kataib Hezbollah about control of Jurf al-Sakhar, where oil smuggling was allegedly taking place, staved off a potential confrontation between the two sides.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Deadly fire engulfs power station in southern Iraqlist 2 of 3What is Iraq’s Jurf al-Sakhar and what is behind gov’t push to control it?list 3 of 3Iraqi forces deploy to Jurf al-Sakhar after deal with Iran-backed groupend of list
It is the latest episode in Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s push to assert federal government control over the country and crack down on corruption, which is allegedly funding pro-Iran militias.
So how does Thursday’s compromise bode for the Iraqi state’s mission to rein in militias and weapons outside its control?
What happened at Jurf al-Sakhar?
Kataib Hezbollah seized Jurf al-Sakhar from ISIL (ISIS) in 2014, renaming it Jurf al-Nasr (“victory”). For the 12 years since then, it has prevented state authorities from re-establishing control and allegedly siphoned oil from local pipelines.
After an intelligence report was released this week about oil smuggling in Jurf al-Sakhar, the government formed a high-level committee to investigate the issue.
